tldr: When injecting low-dimensional robot signals (such as actions and proprioception) into pretrained video diffusion models, packing them into the frequency domain (DCT) across separate channel bands folds everything into a single "meta-frame." This aligns neatly with the model's prior, cuts inference latency by 39%, and improves task success rates.

(a) Heterogeneous robot signals (e.g., actions, proprioception) are mapped to disjoint DCT frequency bands, unified into a single meta-frame, and routed across policy, world-model, and value prediction tasks. (b) Measuring the relative reconstruction error with a frozen video denoiser reveals that DCT encoding stays closest to the model's prior (lowest error) compared to conventional spatial duplicate and VAE embeddings.
overview:
World Action Models (WAMs), which adapt pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) for robot control, are gaining significant attention. Because video models possess rich internal knowledge of physical scene dynamics, they serve as a powerful backbone for jointly predicting future visual observations and robot actions. However, a major hurdle remains: how to design the interface for injecting low-dimensional robot signals (such as joint angles/proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space originally sculpted by natural videos.

Prior approaches typically treated this signal injection as a mere formatting detail. They either tiled signals across full spatial dimensions—consuming multiple dedicated latent frames—or bolted on specialized encoders and decoders. However, adding latent frames causes the computational cost of self-attention to grow quadratically, while extra modules can disrupt the pretrained backbone weights. To address this, the authors introduce a fresh perspective: signal injection is fundamentally a distribution-alignment problem regarding how well an input matches the denoising prior of the video diffusion model.

Diagnostics reveal that conventional methods—which spatially tile numerical values into grids—appear highly "unnatural" (out-of-distribution) to video models and trigger heavy corrections from a frozen denoiser. In contrast, embedding signals onto smooth cosine bases via the frequency domain (Discrete Cosine Transform: DCT) blends remarkably well into the video model's prior. Motivated by this insight, the authors introduce "MetaWAM." It packs all robot signals into disjoint frequency channel bands within a single latent frame and projects them to spatial latents using an analytical inverse DCT. This setup requires no additional neural networks and enables signal reconstruction through purely invertible, analytical operations.

Evaluated on RoboCasa, LIBERO benchmarks, and three real-world precision manipulation tasks on a Franka Panda robot, MetaWAM reduces latent frame count and cuts inference latency by roughly 39%, while consistently outperforming prior methods in task success rates.
contributions: Reframing robot signal injection in World Action Models not as an arbitrary formatting problem, but as a distribution-alignment problem with the prior of pretrained video models.

Experimentally demonstrating—using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen video denoiser as a diagnostic probe—that frequency-domain packing aligns far better with the video model's prior than spatial duplication.

Proposing the "unified meta-frame" interface (MetaWAM), which multiplexes all robot signals into a single frame and decodes them analytically without requiring added encoders, decoders, or architectural modifications.

Demonstrating both computational efficiency gains (a 39% reduction in inference latency via sequence length reduction) and superior task success rates (e.g., 85.0% on real-world tasks) across simulations (RoboCasa, LIBERO) and physical robot platforms.

sections.heading: How Can We Naturally Fit Robot Signals into Video Models?
sections.summary: In World Action Models built upon video diffusion backbones, injecting low-dimensional robot signals into video latent space has remained a key challenge. Framing this as a distribution-alignment issue, the authors propose MetaWAM, which unifies all signals into a single frame via the frequency domain.
sections.details:
Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combining vision, language, and action have drawn immense interest. However, most remain reactive policies that map observations directly to immediate actions, lacking an explicit internal model of environmental transitions showing how the world shifts in response to their actions. To bridge this gap, research into World Action Models (WAMs)—which leverage pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) to jointly predict future observations and actions—is rapidly progressing.

Yet, building a WAM presents a major barrier: how should we inject structured, low-dimensional signals like robot joint angles (proprioception), actions (action chunks), and values into a latent space shaped entirely by the statistics of natural videos?

Conventional techniques have spatially tiled values across full latent frames (Spatial Duplication), rendered trajectories visually before passing them through a pretrained VAE, or attached dedicated external action encoders and decoders. However, tiling inflates the latent sequence length $T$ and causes the self-attention compute to explode quadratically, while extra modules undermine the compatibility of the pretrained backbone.

The authors rethink this issue as a distribution-alignment problem: how naturally does a representation match the prior held by the video model's denoiser? Probing a frozen video denoiser revealed that spatially tiled numerical grids are strongly out-of-distribution and suffer severe corrections. In contrast, latents structured as smooth bases via the frequency domain (Discrete Cosine Transform: DCT) stay exceptionally close to the model's prior.

Based on these findings, the paper introduces "MetaWAM," which multiplexes all robot variables into disjoint frequency bands within a single "meta-frame." Because it relies entirely on analytical inverse DCT lifting and slot-aware unpacking without any learned modules, it simultaneously boosts inference speed and task success rates.

By embedding individual signals into disjoint channel bands in the frequency domain, a single frame handles policy, world-model, and value prediction tasks. As shown in the right plot, at noise level $\sigma=1.0$, DCT encoding achieves the lowest relative reconstruction error compared to conventional spatial duplication and VAE embeddings.

sections.heading: The Evolution of World Action Models and Latent Representations
sections.summary: This section surveys related work across cascaded and joint World Action Models as well as latent signal representations. MetaWAM enhances distribution alignment within the latent representation without modifying the underlying architecture.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into two research streams: World Action Models (WAMs) and Latent Signal Representations.

### World Action Models
WAMs formulate robot control as the joint generative modeling of future states and actions. They broadly follow two design paradigms:
- **Cascaded WAMs**: These use a video model as a visual simulator and then infer actions from the generated future frames using a separate inverse dynamics model or policy.
- **Joint WAMs**: These predict actions, future observations, and values within a single unified generative backbone through a shared denoising process. For example, Cosmos Policy preserves the native video architecture by spending separate latent frames on each signal, whereas DreamZero attaches dedicated action encoders and decoders around the video backbone.

MetaWAM belongs to the family of Joint WAMs, but takes an orthogonal approach. Rather than modifying the network architecture, it fundamentally redesigns how robot signals are represented inside the latent sequence.

### Latent Signal Representations
Prior efforts to compress robot or agent signals into compact latent spaces include training VQ-VAEs to extract discrete action tokens, or applying 1D DCT across temporal action sequences (e.g., FAST). MetaWAM differs in both objective and mechanism. It directly maps heterogeneous robot signals into channel-wise 2D DCT bands tailored for the latent space of pretrained video diffusion models, lifts them into spatial latents via an analytical 2D inverse DCT, and recovers them analytically without any learned decoders.

sections.heading: Which Signal Encoding Do Video Models Actually Prefer?
sections.summary: Using the reconstruction error of a frozen video denoiser as a diagnostic probe, the authors evaluated how well various signal injection schemes match the model's prior. While spatial tiling and quadrant partitioning trigger heavy corrections, frequency packing via DCT incurs minimal modification.
sections.details:
To answer the question, "What form of robot signals will a pretrained video diffusion model accept most naturally?", the authors conducted diagnostic experiments. They measured the Relative Reconstruction Error when latents were fed into a frozen Cosmos-Predict2 denoiser. Normalized by the magnitude of the clean latent, a smaller denoising residual indicates that the input aligns more closely with the model's prior (i.e., is in-distribution).

### Comparing Single-Signal Injections
First, focusing on a single action signal, three methods were compared:
- **Spatial Duplication**: Tiling raw numerical values across the entire frame row-by-row (as used in Cosmos Policy).
- **VAE Encoding**: Plotting trajectories as visual images and passing them through a pretrained VAE.
- **DCT Encoding**: Placing raw numerical values directly into DCT coefficient slots and lifting them into smooth cosine bases across the spatial latent.

The results were striking. Spatial Duplication suffered the highest correction from the denoiser, revealing that constant grid patterns are deeply unnatural to video models. VAE Encoding also failed to lower error; while it passed cleanly through the VAE, the denoiser still treated it as out-of-distribution. In contrast, DCT Encoding achieved substantially lower relative reconstruction error across all noise levels $\sigma \le 5.0$. What matters is not whether an input passes through a VAE, but whether it respects the denoiser's prior.

### Comparing Multi-Signal Packing
Next, the authors evaluated four strategies for packing three signals—action, current state, and value:
- **Separate Spatial Duplication**: Assigning an independent spatial frame to each of the three signals (consuming 3 frames total).
- **Meta-Quadrants**: Dividing a single frame into equal spatial quadrants and tiling each signal within its quadrant.
- **Meta-Compact**: Partitioning a single frame into spatial regions sized proportionally to each signal's dimensionality.
- **Unified Meta-Frame (Proposed)**: Mapping signals to disjoint frequency channel bands rather than spatial partitions, and lifting them to spatial latents via channel-wise 2D inverse DCT.

As shown in Table 1, at noise level $\sigma=1.0$, Meta-Quadrants (0.6730) and Meta-Compact (0.6234) showed worse errors than Separate Spatial Duplication (0.6178). Simply squeezing signals into one frame is not enough; spatial borders and discontinuities introduce harmful artifacts. In contrast, the proposed Unified Meta-Frame achieved the lowest error at 0.5613. It condenses all signals into a single frame while simultaneously maximizing alignment with the denoiser.

captions.F2: Signal injection schemes compared in the diagnostic experiments. (a–c) Single-signal spatial duplication, VAE encoding, and DCT encoding. (d–g) Multi-signal packing strategies: separate frames (d), spatial domain partitioning within one frame (e, f), and the proposed frequency-domain channel packing lifted via 2D inverse DCT (g).

sections.heading: MetaWAM: A Unified Interface via Frequency Meta-Frames
sections.summary: This section details the architecture of MetaWAM, which packs all robot signals into frequency channel bands within a single meta-frame and enables policy, world-model, and value prediction through slot-aware task routing.
sections.details:
MetaWAM preserves the exact architecture of the video diffusion backbone, completely reimagining only the latent interface through which robot signals enter and leave.

### 4.1 Overview: Unified Robot Signal Interface
Conventional WAMs dedicate separate frames to states, actions, future states, and values, inflating the sequence length $T$. MetaWAM introduces two meta-frames—an input frame $z^m_{\mathrm{in}}$ and an output prediction frame $z^m_{\mathrm{out}}$—packaging the full sequence into 8 frames:

$$\mathbf{z} = [z^m_{\mathrm{in}}, z^{w}_{t}, z^{p}_{t}, z^{s}_{t}, z^{w}_{t+\Delta t}, z^{p}_{t+\Delta t}, z^{s}_{t+\Delta t}, z^m_{\mathrm{out}}]$$

Here, $w, p, s$ denote wrist, primary, and side camera views. Furthermore, $z^m_{\mathrm{in}}$ repurposes the leading empty slot inherently allocated by the video tokenizer, introducing zero marginal token overhead. Compared to baseline frame-per-signal injection, this shrinks the pairwise self-attention compute by roughly 47%.

### 4.2 Distribution-Aware Spectral Lifting
Within each meta-frame, the channel dimension is partitioned into dedicated bands for each signal. Normalized robot signals $q$ are written directly into assigned frequency slots (the $k_H=0$ row) within their respective channel bands, with unused entries zero-padded. An orthonormal 2D inverse DCT ($\mathcal{T}^{-1}_{\mathrm{2D}}$) is then applied channel-wise to lift them into the spatial latent $z^m$. After denoising, the original signals are cleanly extracted from the output meta-frame by applying a standard 2D DCT and reading out the designated slots. No trainable decoders are needed.

### 4.3 & 4.4 Slot-Aware Task Routing
MetaWAM simultaneously trains policy learning (predicting actions from state), world modeling (predicting future state from state and action), and value prediction (predicting return from the full transition) within a single model. These tasks operate over the exact same set of variables, differing only in causal direction (which variables are inputs vs. targets).
Thus, while keeping the variable layout inside the meta-frame fixed, MetaWAM uses a slot mask $M_{\mathrm{slot}}$ to designate channel bands as either clean conditioning inputs or denoising prediction targets depending on the task. For policy samples, only the state band is treated as conditioning, while the action band onward serves as prediction targets. This fine-grained channel control keeps tasks cleanly separated despite sharing a single frame.

### 4.5 Training Objectives
In addition to the standard diffusion denoising loss across the sequence, MetaWAM applies a Huber loss ($\delta=1$) on the analytically unpacked actions, future states, and values as an auxiliary objective. Furthermore, an off-slot penalty $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{off}}$ (weighted by $\lambda_{\mathrm{off}}=10^{-4}$) penalizes spurious energy appearing outside designated slot coordinates, suppressing unwanted frequency artifacts.

captions.F3: Overall architecture of MetaWAM. Top left: normalized signals are placed as 1D DCT coefficients and lifted into a smooth spatial meta-frame via 2D inverse DCT. Bottom: slot-aware task routing dynamically switches conditioning and target masks across policy, world-model, and value prediction while maintaining an identical meta-frame layout.

sections.heading: Empirical Superiority and Efficiency in Simulation and the Real World
sections.summary: MetaWAM was benchmarked on RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a physical Franka Panda. It achieved a 68.9% success rate on RoboCasa while slashing inference latency by 39%, and reached 85.0% success on the physical robot. Ablations confirm the clear advantage of frequency representations.
sections.details:
Using Cosmos-Predict2-2B-Video2World as the generative backbone, the authors thoroughly evaluated MetaWAM in simulation and on hardware.

### 5.1 Simulation Benchmarks
- **RoboCasa**: Evaluated across 24 static kitchen tasks in a low-data regime (only 50 demonstrations per task). MetaWAM achieved an average success rate of **68.9%**, outperforming the matched Cosmos Policy baseline and rivaling methods trained on orders of magnitude more data. Compressing multiple frames into one not only avoided performance penalties, but actively boosted success.
- **LIBERO / LIBERO-Plus**: MetaWAM attained a **98.1%** average success rate across standard LIBERO-4 suites. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations spanning seven distinct shifts (viewpoint, initial state, language, lighting, background, noise, layout), it scored an overall success rate of **83.44%**—the highest among all evaluated WAMs. It exhibited notable robustness against camera viewpoint shifts (82.93%) and paraphrased instructions (89.56%).

### 5.2 Real-World Franka Panda Experiments
Using a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda arm equipped with three cameras (wrist, primary, side), three manipulation tasks were tested: "Sweep" (sweeping blocks into a dustpan), "Place Cup" (setting a cup onto a coaster), and "Build Block" (stacking cubes). MetaWAM achieved an **85.0%** success rate on in-distribution (ID) setups and **68.3%** under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts involving obstacles and background changes, consistently surpassing Cosmos Policy.

### 5.3 Ablation Studies
Detailed comparisons on RoboCasa highlighted several key takeaways:
- **Inference Speed**: While the baseline using separate frames required 0.479s per query, MetaWAM dropped latency to **0.291s (a ~39% reduction)**.
- **Packing Methods**: Under identical single-frame latency constraints, spatial packing (Meta-Quadrants: 60.1%, Meta-Compact: 61.3%) lagged far behind MetaWAM's frequency-domain approach (**68.9%**).
- **Multitask Benefits**: Beyond policy performance, MetaWAM also recorded superior numbers in world-model visual quality (PSNR), future state normalized error (NEE), and value prediction mean absolute error (MAE).

captions.F4: Rollouts across three real-world tasks on the Franka Panda (Sweep, Build Block, Place Cup). From left to right: target task trajectories, imagined future visual trajectories generated by the model, and actual executed robot rollouts, showing highly aligned and consistent motions.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: The paper demonstrates the power of framing signal injection as distribution alignment and packing data into the frequency domain. Adapting the fixed band layout dynamically and improving language grounding remain promising avenues for future work.
sections.details:
This study reframes robot signal injection in World Action Models as a distribution-alignment challenge with the prior of pretrained video models. Guided by diagnostic evaluations with a frozen denoiser, the authors established that frequency-domain packing is far superior to traditional spatial tiling, culminating in the training-free, analytical "MetaWAM" interface.

### Limitations
- **Fixed Band Layout**: The channel allocations and loss weights assigned to signals are currently fixed, which may require manual tuning when adapting to tasks with vastly different signal dimensions or scales.
- **Language Grounding**: Limitations inherited from the Cosmos-Predict2 backbone constrain fine-grained instruction following, leaving room for integration with stronger vision-language foundation models.
- **Visual Context Shifts**: In LIBERO-Plus experiments, the policy exhibited sensitivity to drastic background swaps and initial robot pose shifts.

sections.heading: Appendix: Generalization Across Backbones and Real-World OOD Behaviors
sections.summary: Diagnostic findings hold across other modern video backbones such as Wan2.1 and Wan2.2, while qualitative rollouts confirm robust physical robot execution under challenging out-of-distribution conditions.
sections.details:
### Validation Across Alternative Video Backbones
To verify whether these findings generalize beyond Cosmos-Predict2, identical diagnostic experiments were conducted on Flow Matching backbones, including Wan2.1-I2V-14B and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. Across model scales and training objectives, DCT encoding and the Unified Meta-Frame consistently outperformed spatial baselines in reconstruction accuracy across all noise levels. This confirms that the benefits of frequency packing reflect an intrinsic property common to video diffusion architectures.

### Qualitative Evaluation in Real-World OOD Environments
Real-world OOD evaluations introduced diverse physical disturbances, including distractor objects in the workspace, large offsets in initial object placements, and modified table backgrounds or lighting. Visualizations in the appendix show that despite these visual and spatial domain shifts, MetaWAM avoids failure modes, generating coherent and smooth manipulation trajectories to complete the tasks.

captions.F7: Real-world rollout examples under out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Even when distractor objects are present or table backgrounds and object starting positions change drastically, MetaWAM generates robust, uncorrupted action trajectories.

takeaways: When injecting low-dimensional numbers into video models, lifting them smoothly via the frequency domain (DCT) aligns far better with the model's prior than forcing them into stretched spatial grids.
When merging multiple robot signals into a single frame, spatial quadrant partitioning creates disruptive edge boundaries; allocating signals across frequency channel bands is far more effective.
Shortening the sequence length cuts the quadratic overhead of self-attention, offering significant practical value by slashing inference latency by roughly 40%.
Analytical orthogonal transforms (DCT / iDCT) eliminate the need for learned encoders and decoders while delivering higher accuracy and faster training convergence.
limitations: The fixed channel band allocation requires manual re-engineering when applying the interface to robots with vastly different degrees of freedom or new sensor inputs.
Inherited characteristics from the underlying Cosmos-Predict2 backbone leave minor vulnerabilities when handling complex language instructions or sudden background texture shifts.
Real-world validation remains focused on three tabletop tasks, leaving scalability to higher-dimensional setups—such as bimanual coordination or mobile manipulation—to future work.
